title: Timestep-Scalable Spiking Networks
one_liner: SNNs get worse when you give them more time to compute, and this paper fixes it by replaying old memories and forgetting on schedule.
lead: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are brains' cousins: instead of outputting smooth numbers, they output pulses, like neurons do. They run efficiently on special hardware, but they have a bizarre problem: when you give them more timesteps (more time to think), they get worse, not better, because the training signal shrinks to nearly nothing over long sequences and memory explodes with stale junk. This paper traces the problem and proposes a fix: replay old state to refresh the training signal, and schedule forgetting to purge buildup.

problem.h2: The paradox: more time makes SNNs dumber
paras: SNNs output discrete pulses instead of smooth numbers, like real neurons do. Training them is tricky because pulse generation is not smooth—there's no gradient to follow. Instead, researchers use a trick called surrogate gradients: they pretend the pulse operation is smooth during training, then use the fake gradients to update the network.

When you run an SNN, you unroll it over many timesteps (many little time slices). Intuitively, more timesteps should let the network think longer and learn richer dynamics. But the opposite happens: past a certain point, adding more timesteps crashes accuracy. This is the timestep scaling paradox. A beginner would expect longer sequences to help the network learn temporal patterns better because more time lets the network represent finer distinctions, but in fact two invisible killers strike: the training signal shrinks to near-zero at early timesteps (so the network cannot update its early decisions because training cannot tell what went wrong that far back), and memory piles up without limit (so neurons get drowned out by noise because they cannot distinguish fresh signals from stale garbage).

callout.html: When you train SNNs over many timesteps, gradients grow faint at the start and information from earlier timesteps stops reaching the neuron updates, so adding more timesteps actually degrades learning.

panels.title: 1. Setup: SNN unrolls over time
panels.caption: An SNN rolls out the same neuron over timesteps t0, t1, t2, t3, t4.

panels.title: 2. The problem: early state leaks out
panels.caption: Gradient from t4 step backward; early timesteps get vanishingly small gradients.

panels.title: 3. Memory buildup: state piles on state
panels.viz_args: Each timestep adds to memory without dumping it; state explodes.
panels.caption: Neurons accumulate old history they cannot use, drowning out new signals.

panels.title: 4. The paper's move: replay and truncate
panels.caption: Memory reconsolidation plays back old state; forgetting cuts accumulation path.

panels.title: 5. Payoff: gradient flows, memory stays sane
panels.caption: Gradients now healthy across timesteps; more timesteps help, not hurt.

steps.b: Step 1: Set up the spiking neuron
steps.text: A neuron accumulates charge over time and fires when charge crosses a threshold.
The same neuron state evolves: each step adds new input and decays or stores charge.

steps.b: Step 3: Replay old state as memory reconsolidation
steps.text: Periodically, force the neuron to output its stored state again, so gradients can flow backward through old memories.
At set intervals, reset the accumulation path to zero, purging stale buildup and stopping memory from exploding.
Gradients now propagate freely from late timesteps back to early ones, so training can learn from longer sequences.

paras: The paper modifies the spiking neuron's internal state evolution rule. Normally, a neuron accumulates charge and fires; here, the authors add two new operations: a memory replay mechanism that outputs stored state at schedule points, and a periodic reset that cuts off the accumulation chain.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: temporal gradient strength
hidden.name: Gradient magnitude across timesteps
paras: As you backpropagate through time in an SNN, the gradient (the update signal) shrinks with each step backward. Early timesteps get near-zero gradients, so the network cannot learn to use long-term patterns. This decay is the core killer.

The paper measures this implicitly by running the network on tasks that need long-term temporal memory. When gradient fades early, accuracy on those tasks crashes because the network cannot update weights that affect early decisions, so those early choices stay wrong. When gradients stay healthy, accuracy improves proportionally because each weight can be nudged in the right direction no matter when it acts. The paper does not plot gradients explicitly, but the accuracy gains are evidence that the mechanism works—strong gradients at early timesteps that let training fix early mistakes.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger gradient signal at that timestep. Without the fix, only late timesteps (t=3 to 6) get good signal; early steps are nearly black.

reads.html: Imagine shouting a secret to a person standing very far away. At the moment you shout, the sound is loud. By the time it reaches them, it is a whisper. They cannot hear you. Backprop through many timesteps in an SNN is like that whisper: the training signal dies before it reaches early decisions.

Long-term temporal gradient vanishing refers to the exponential decay of gradients as they propagate backward through long unrolled sequences in recurrent networks, preventing the network from learning dependencies that span many timesteps.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the two-part repair
paras: The paper has two problems to solve. First: gradients fade because the chain of computation is too long, so early states do not get nudged during training. Solution: memory reconsolidation. Periodically, the neuron outputs its stored state again (as a replay). This replay creates a new gradient path from the loss back to that stored state, so old memories get updated even though they happened early in time. It is like rewinding a tape and playing a song again so every note gets heard.

Second: as you add more timesteps, neurons accumulate charge endlessly—the internal memory grows so large it drowns out new signals. The network tries to learn with huge noisy state values instead of clean ones. Solution: temporal forgetting. At schedule points, reset the accumulation path to zero. This purge prevents explosion, keeps state values in a healthy range, and actually makes gradients cleaner because they do not have to squeeze through noise from past buildup. Together, replay makes old memories trainable, and forgetting keeps new memories sane.

stages.s: Neuron adds input to stored charge
Temporal forgetting: zero out accumulation at schedule time
Fire spike if charge crosses threshold
Output spike; gradients now flow through replayed state too

math.h2: The equation: state update with replay and forgetting
math.words: Neuron state at next timestep equals current state plus input minus leak, with periodic replay outputs and truncation
math.equation: V(t+1) = V(t) + I(t) - leak * V(t) + reconsolidate(V) - truncate(t) * V(t)
symbols: neuron membrane voltage at timestep t
incoming input signal at timestep t
decay rate, how fast old state fades
replay mechanism: output stored state periodically to create new gradient paths
temporal forgetting: set to 1 at schedule times to zero state, else 0

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose V(0) = 0, and input pulses arrive: I(1)=10, I(2)=5, I(3)=8, leak=0.1, no replay or truncate yet.
V(3) = 14 + 8 - 0.1*14 = 20.6. Charge keeps growing—a gradient trying to update V(1) now sees 0.1^2 = 0.01 decay on top of path length.
With truncate at t=2: V(2_after) = 0. Restart. V(3) = 0 + 8 - 0 = 8. New gradient from V(3) is 100x stronger reaching back to V(2_after), and V(2_after) can be updated.
With reconsolidate: at t=3, also output V_old from t=1. Training then has a direct gradient path to that old state from the loss, not through decay.

math.note: The equation shows state evolution; reconsolidate and truncate are the two new pieces that fix the gradient and memory problems.

bars.h2: Comparison: standard SNN versus the fix

charts.title: Standard SNN (timestep scaling paradox)
charts.note: More timesteps hurt because gradients vanish and state explodes. Accuracy crashes.

charts.title: Timestep-Scalable (TS) neuron (this paper)
charts.note: Memory replay and forgetting keep gradients healthy and state bounded. More timesteps help learning because the network can now update its early decisions (replay preserves gradient flow) and work with clean state values (forgetting prevents explosion).

items.html: If you truncate the state too often, the neuron forgets useful patterns and cannot integrate information over time. The network has memory but loses temporal coherence, like a brain resetting every second.
If you truncate too rarely, state accumulation returns; memory still explodes and gradients still vanish. The fix only works if the schedule is tuned to the task.

items.b: Reconsolidation replayed state clashes with current dynamics.
items.html: Replaying old state creates an artificial path that may conflict with the natural forward evolution. If not designed carefully, this can confuse gradient flow rather than help it because the replay output signal may contradict what the network naturally evolved to at that point, creating noisy conflicting updates.

Tune the truncation schedule to the maximum temporal dependency in the task (e.g., if events span 50 timesteps, truncate at 50). Validate that early-timestep gradients are healthy by checking that loss decreases smoothly during training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy SNN on a synthetic temporal task: e.g., an input that carries a signal at timestep 2, and the network must remember it and output a spike at timestep 10. Train two versions: standard SNN and TS-neuron SNN. Run both for 5, 10, 20, and 50 timesteps. Plot accuracy on the y-axis and timestep count on the x-axis.
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy = (number of correct decisions) / (total number of timesteps)
demo.closing: The standard version should show a sharp drop as timesteps increase (accuracy crashes because gradients vanish and memory explodes); the TS version should climb or stay flat (accuracy improves or holds steady because replay keeps gradients alive and forgetting keeps memory bounded), proving that more time actually helps when you fix the two killers.
